body: The spec is commendably explicit about assumptions, but several definitions do not support the inferences drawn from them. (1) FR-012/SC-004 require a correlation between ImbalanceScore and performance degradation, but the design yields at most a handful of units (three properties × two or three databases). With n ≈ 3–9, no meaningful correlation coefficient can be estimated; the 'causal link' language in SC-004 overstates what a correlation over so few units could establish even in principle. (2) The ImbalanceScore itself is underdefined: a Gini coefficient of cluster counts from K-Means (k=50) depends on arbitrary k, random initialization, and the L2-normalized Magpie space; it is not stated whether it is computed per dataset, per property, or per chemistry, and it is not comparable across datasets of different sizes. (3) The Gini coefficient of a continuous target distribution (FR-011) measures dispersion, not imbalance in the sense of under-represented regions; a uniform target distribution and a Gaussian one can share a Gini-like spread while having very different tail density. This conflates two distinct notions. (4) SMOTE on compositional descriptors interpolates between chemically distinct materials, producing feature vectors corresponding to no real composition; the CV ≤ 0.30 allowance for the synthetic portion means the 'balanced' condition may be balanced by physically meaningless data, which threatens the interpretation of any performance difference. (5) The SHAP validation via synthetic ground truth (FR-014) tests SHAP on a synthetic model, not on the materials models; it cannot validate that SHAP rankings are physically meaningful in the real pipeline — only that the SHAP implementation recovers known weights under conditions unlike the actual data. (6) The 'bottom [deferred]' placeholders in US-2, FR-010, and SC-001 leave the primary evaluation subset undefined; until resolved, the central measurable outcome is not well specified. Finally, the power analysis (FR-015) determines the number of seeds for detecting a fixed effect size, but the paired tests compare two models on the same splits — the relevant variance is across splits, and Cohen's d = 0.5 as a 'medium' effect is asserted without justification for MAE differences.
